title: Does a Circuit Need Its Protein Later?

scenes.tts: A circuit has to be built. It also has to be kept running. Picture a circuit that was built without one key protein. Now switch that protein on in an adult. Can that undo the damage? If the wiring was built wrong, it stays wrong. If the wiring is sound but needs the protein to keep working, the circuit should recover.
scenes.visual: A circuit builds with an empty slot for a key protein; the protein arrives in an adult; it splits into the two possible answers, built wrong versus needs the protein to keep working.
scenes.narration: A circuit has to be built. It also has to be kept running. Picture a circuit that was built without one key protein. Now switch that protein on in an adult. Can that undo the damage? If the wiring was built wrong, it stays wrong. If the wiring is sound but needs the protein to keep working, the circuit should recover.

scenes.tts: Rett syndrome puts this question to the test. Girls with Rett syndrome seem to develop typically for many months. Then they lose purposeful hand use and speech. Most cases come from mutations in a gene called M E C P 2. The gene makes a protein that binds D N A where the cytosines carry methyl groups.

Most cases come from mutations in a gene called MECP2. The gene makes a protein that binds DNA where the cytosines carry methyl groups.
scenes.visual: A timeline with a green typical stretch then a red loss stretch; then the MECP2 gene makes a MeCP2 protein chip that lands on a DNA line with methyl tags.

scenes.tts: Now look at mice that lack this gene. They appear typical for several weeks. Then they develop tremor, breathing changes and reduced movement. Their neurons do not die in large numbers. Instead the neurons are smaller, with simpler dendrites.
scenes.visual: A mouse timeline with typical then symptoms and three symptom chips; then two neurons side by side, a typical one and a smaller, simpler one.
scenes.narration: Now look at mice that lack this gene. They appear typical for several weeks. Then they develop tremor, breathing changes and reduced movement. Their neurons do not die in large numbers. Instead the neurons are smaller, with simpler dendrites.

scenes.tts: In two thousand seven, Jacky Guy, Adrian Bird and colleagues built mice in which the gene is silent. A blocking sequence sits inside it. The mice also carry an enzyme called Cre. Cre enters the nucleus only after the mouse receives the drug tamoxifen. Then Cre removes the block, and the gene comes back on. So the team chooses when the gene returns.
scenes.visual: A nucleus holds a gene bar with a red block on it; tamoxifen arrives and Cre moves into the nucleus, lifts the block off, and the gene turns green.
scenes.narration: In two thousand seven, Jacky Guy, Adrian Bird and colleagues built mice in which the gene is silent. A blocking sequence sits inside it. The mice also carry an enzyme called Cre. Cre enters the nucleus only after the mouse receives the drug tamoxifen. Then Cre removes the block, and the gene comes back on. So the team chooses when the gene returns.

scenes.tts: This is the key test. The team treated adult mice that already had symptoms. They gave tamoxifen, which restored M E C P 2. Many symptoms reversed, in young adult mice and in older adult mice. In mice without the silenced gene, tamoxifen did nothing.
scenes.caption: This is the key test. The team treated adult mice that already had symptoms. They gave tamoxifen, which restored MeCP2. Many symptoms reversed, in young adult mice and in older adult mice. In mice without the silenced gene, tamoxifen did nothing.
scenes.visual: A symptom curve against age rises, then falls after a tamoxifen marker; tags for young adult and older adult mice; a flat control line for mice without the silenced gene.
scenes.narration: This is the key test. The team treated adult mice that already had symptoms. They gave tamoxifen, which restored MeCP2. Many symptoms reversed, in young adult mice and in older adult mice. In mice without the silenced gene, tamoxifen did nothing.

scenes.tts: So in these mice, the circuits were not permanently miswired. They formed without M E C P 2, and they worked again when it returned. M E C P 2 is needed continuously. This is a mouse result. Whether it holds for an older person is not known. Too much M E C P 2 is also harmful, so the dose matters. Circuits need some proteins to keep running, not only to be built.
